title: The system: a photo and video app built around an object store
caption: The API only grants permission and keeps metadata; bytes go straight from the phone to the store, store events drive the processing, and viewers read through the CDN.

steps.text: The app asks to upload a photo. The API checks auth and quota, writes a pending row, and signs a URL that allows one PUT to one key for 15 minutes.
The app sends the bytes straight to the object store (multipart for videos). No API server ever holds them.
The store emits ObjectCreated to a queue. The event carries the bucket and key, not the bytes.
Workers read the original, write renditions under derived keys (p_77/1080.webp, p_77/hls/…) and mark the row ready.
Viewers fetch through the CDN. Keys never change, so edges cache them for a year; a miss costs one origin GET.
A lifecycle rule moves originals nobody has opened for 90 days to a cheaper tier; renditions stay hot.

scenarios.name: New Year upload spike
scenarios.summary: Uploads jump 10× at midnight: the store absorbs the bytes, and the queue turns the spike into a backlog instead of an outage.

steps.text: Millions of phones upload at 00:00. The API only signs URLs, about 1 ms of work each.
The object store takes the parallel PUTs; random photo ids spread the keys, so no single prefix is hot.
Events queue up faster than workers drain them: a backlog of 40 minutes builds.
Workers autoscale on queue depth. Until a photo is ready, the app shows its own local copy.

scenarios.name: Thumbnailer bug
scenarios.summary: A deploy crashes on one image format: those events retry, land in dead letters, and are replayed after the fix.

steps.text: A new thumbnailer version crashes on every HEIC photo.
Each HEIC event is retried 5 times with backoff, then moved to dead letters; other photos keep flowing.
Those rows stay pending; the app shows a placeholder. The original is safe in the store.
Roll back, replay the dead letters, and the renditions appear. Workers are idempotent by key, so replays are harmless.

scenarios.name: New rendition size
scenarios.summary: Product wants a 2048 px WebP for new tablets: backfill billions of photos without hurting live uploads, or render on demand.

steps.text: Add 2048 px to the thumbnailer for every new upload.
Backfill: list keys by prefix in batches and enqueue synthetic events at a fixed rate, at low priority.
Or render lazily: on a CDN miss for a missing size, generate it once and store it; old photos that nobody views never cost anything.
Cold-tier originals cost a retrieval fee to read, so skip them or render them only on demand.
